# The ear

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Ear, nose, and throat > Basics of ENT > The ear*

[Original Article Link](/library/dp0ooS)

---

## Summary

The ear is the organ of <u>hearing</u> and balance. It is divided into three sections: the outer, the middle, and the <u>inner ear</u>. The <u>outer ear</u> comprises the <u>auricle</u> (<u>pinna</u>), <u>external auditory meatus</u> (auditory canal), and <u>tympanic membrane</u> (<u>eardrum</u>), which separates the <u>outer ear</u> from the <u>middle ear</u>. The <u>middle ear</u> is a hollow structure that comprises the <u>tympanic cavity</u>, the <u>ossicles</u>, and the <u>eustachian tube</u>. The <u>eustachian tube</u> connects the <u>middle ear</u> to the <u>nasopharynx</u>, equalizing the pressure between the <u>middle ear</u> and the atmosphere. The <u>auricle</u> captures sound waves and directs them through the <u>external auditory canal</u> towards the <u>tympanic membrane</u>, thus setting it in motion. The <u>ossicles</u> amplify the resulting vibrations and transmit them to the <u>inner ear</u> via the <u>oval window</u>. The <u>inner ear</u> is a fluid-filled cavity that contains the <u>organ of Corti</u> and the <u>vestibular system</u>. The <u>organ of Corti</u> is responsible for sound detection, and it transmits auditory information to the <u>brain</u> via the cochlear nerve, while the <u>vestibular system</u> is responsible for the registration of body movement and spatial orientation. It transmits information to the <u>brain</u> via the vestibular nerve.

---

## Outer ear

* Definition: the external portion of the ear

* Parts

* <u>Auricle</u> (pinna) 

* Structure

* The only visible part of the ear

* Consists of <u>elastic cartilage</u>

* Function: collects sound waves; important for directional <u>hearing</u>

* External auditory meatus (auditory canal)

* Structure

* The outer third is formed by <u>cartilage</u>, the inner two thirds are formed by bone.

* Lined by thin <u>keratinized stratified squamous epithelium</u> along the entire canal; also covers the external <u>tympanic membrane</u>.

* <u>Epithelium</u> contains ceruminous glands that produce cerumen (<u>ear wax</u>): yellow-brownish, waxy, <u>bactericidal</u> secretion.

* Function: transmission of sound waves to the <u>tympanic membrane</u>

* Tympanic membrane (<u>eardrum</u>)

* Structure

* Thin, cone-shaped membrane

* Cutaneous outer, fibrous middle, and mucous inner layer

* Umbo: the point where <u>ossicles</u> attach to the <u>tympanic membrane</u>

* Cone of light: a cone-shaped light reflection of the otoscope light in the <u>anterior</u> inferior quadrant, which helps with orientation

* Function: Sound waves cause vibration of the <u>tympanic membrane</u>, which in turn transmits these vibrations to the <u>ossicles</u> of the <u>middle ear</u> (i.e., the <u>malleus</u>, <u>incus</u>, and <u>stapes</u>).





> [!NOTE]
> The area behind the <u>auricle</u> and the <u>external auditory canal</u> are innervated by the glossopharyngeal and <u>vagus nerve</u>. Mechanical cleansing of the <u>external auditory canal</u> can lead to <u>nausea</u> and <u>coughing</u>!

## Middle ear

* Definition: : The middle portion of the ear that is located internal to the <u>tympanic membrane</u> and external to the <u>oval window</u> of the <u>inner ear</u>.

* Consists of: <u>tympanic cavity</u>, epitympanic recess, <u>mastoid process</u>, and <u>eustachian tube</u>

* Function: transmits sound waves from the air to the <u>ossicles</u> and then to the <u>inner ear</u>





![Outer, middle, and inner ear](media/vagep6wq1df6jfsypcrpy88a.jpg)

Outer, middle, and inner ear




### Parts




#### Tympanic cavity




* Air-filled space that is located within the petrous portion of the <u>temporal bone</u>

* Contains <u>ossicles</u>, muscles, and nerves

* Connected to the <u>nasopharyngeal</u> cavity via the <u>eustachian tube</u>

* Oval window 

* An opening located in the <u>middle ear</u> at the base of the <u>cochlea</u> through which sound waves are transmitted to the <u>inner ear</u>

* Covered by the footplate of the <u>stapes</u>

* Round window 

* A membrane-covered opening in the <u>middle ear</u> that lies below the <u>stapes</u>-covered <u>oval window</u>.

* Vibrations of the footplate of the <u>stapes</u> are transmitted to the <u>round window</u> through the <u>perilymph</u>, which causes it to vibrate in the opposite phase of the <u>oval window</u>.

* Injury to the <u>round window</u> (e.g., violent nose blowing, <u>barotrauma</u> while diving) causes <u>sensorineural hearing loss</u>.





![Tympanic cavity](media/uno08v4fmlnwclwmlzym3faq.jpg)

Tympanic cavity




#### Auditory ossicles




* Three small bones in the <u>middle ear</u> that form a chain of bones connecting the <u>tympanic membrane</u> laterally to the <u>oval window</u> of the <u>inner ear</u> medially 

* <u>Malleus</u>: inserts laterally into the <u>tympanic membrane</u>; the most <u>lateral</u> <u>ossicle</u>

* <u>Incus</u>: connects to the <u>malleus</u> laterally and to the <u>stapes</u> medially

* <u>Stapes</u>: inserts medially into the membrane of the <u>oval window</u>; the most <u>medial</u> <u>ossicle</u>

* Function: : The <u>ossicles</u> receive the acoustic vibrations from the <u>tympanic membrane</u> and amplify them; . They then transmit the amplified acoustic vibrations to the fluid of the <u>inner ear</u> via the <u>oval window</u> with minimal energy loss.





![Borders of the tympanic cavity](media/kwnhma9dg3fdtvzjmym7c6op.jpg)

Borders of the tympanic cavity

![Ossicles (middle ear)](media/eiqkx57kf7efu3sv8r6uie11.jpg)

Ossicles (middle ear)




#### Eustachian tube (<u>pharyngotympanic tube</u>)




* Definition: connects the <u>middle ear</u> cavity with the <u>nasopharynx</u>

* Function:

* Controls the pressure within the <u>middle ear</u> and allows the pressure to be equalized on both sides of the <u>tympanic membrane</u> (e.g., important for altitude compensation)

* Usually closed but opens when chewing, <u>swallowing</u>, or yawning (ear clearing)





> [!NOTE]
> During and after a cold, the <u>eustachian tube</u> can become blocked by swelling of the <u>mucosa</u> and mucus impaction. This often results in dull <u>hearing</u>, <u>pain</u>, and a feeling of pressure or fullness in the affected ear.




#### Tensor tympani muscle



* A <u>skeletal muscle</u> that attaches to the <u>malleus</u>

* Origin: <u>cartilaginous</u> and bony margins of the <u>eustachian tube</u>

* Insertion: handle of the <u>malleus</u>

* Action: : Contraction of the muscle pulls the <u>malleus</u> medially. This action tenses the <u>tympanic membrane</u> and damps vibration in the <u>ear ossicles</u>, resulting in a reduction of the perceived amplitude of sound.

* Innervation: medial pterygoid nerve, a branch from the <u>mandibular nerve</u> (V3)




#### Stapedius muscle



* The smallest <u>skeletal muscle</u> in the human body; attaches to the <u>stapes</u>

* Origin: pyramidal eminence (hollow protrusion from the <u>posterior</u> wall of the <u>tympanic membrane</u>)

* Insertion: neck of the <u>stapes</u>

* Action: : contraction of the muscle pulls the neck of the <u>stapes</u> laterally, thereby damping the vibrations of the <u>stapes</u>;  and allowing it to control the amplitude of sound waves being transmitted to the <u>inner ear</u>.

* Innervation: : the nerve to stapedius, a branch from the <u>facial nerve</u>




> [!NOTE]
> The <u>stapedius muscle</u> dampens transmission of loud noises to the <u>inner ear</u> (acoustic or stapedial reflex). <u>Stapedius</u> <u>weakness</u> (e.g., due to <u>Bell palsy</u>) can result in hyperacusis (increased <u>sensitivity</u> to environmental sounds, which can also result from <u>ear trauma</u> or middle/<u>inner ear</u> infection)




#### Mastoid process




* Process of the <u>temporal bone</u> behind the ear

* Becomes pneumatized (aerated) with age, with mastoid air cells formation





> [!NOTE]
> A <u>middle ear</u> infection can spread to neighboring structures and result in <u>perforation of the tympanic membrane</u>, <u>labyrinthitis</u>, <u>mastoiditis</u>, <u>cerebral venous sinus thrombosis</u>, and <u>meningitis</u>.

## Inner ear

* Definition: : The innermost portion of the ear that contains organs of <u>hearing</u> (i.e., <u>cochlea</u>) and equilibrium (i.e., vestibule) and is situated within the petrous part of the <u>temporal bone</u>.




![Anatomy of the inner ear](media/nvo9aikpclf0e3z1azhy21jf.jpg)

Anatomy of the inner ear




### Parts




#### Labyrinth




* It is subdivided into

* Osseous labyrinth (<u>bony labyrinth</u>)

* The bony wall of the <u>inner ear</u> in the <u>temporal bone</u>

* Contains the vestibule, the three <u>semicircular canals</u>, and the <u>cochlea</u>

* Lined with <u>periosteum</u>

* Membranous labyrinth

* Lodged within the <u>osseous labyrinth</u> in perilymph (low <u>potassium</u>, high <u>sodium</u>; transmits sound vibrations from the <u>stapes</u>-covered <u>oval window</u> to the <u>round window</u>)

* Filled with endolymph (high <u>potassium</u>, low <u>sodium</u>)

* Contains sensory organs

* Contains complex series of fluid-filled spaces

* Vestibular duct (<u>scala vestibuli</u>): filled with <u>perilymph</u>; begins at <u>oval window</u>; connected with <u>tympanic duct</u> at helicotrema (passage at apical end of <u>cochlea</u>)

* Cochlear duct (<u>scala media</u>): filled with endolymph; contains spiral <u>organ of Corti</u> and auditory <u>hair</u> cells

* Tympanic duct (<u>scala tympani</u>): filled with <u>perilymph</u>; ends at <u>round window</u>





#### Cochlea




* Fluid-filled, snail-shaped cavity in the labyrinth

* Layers of the <u>cochlea</u> 

* Bone

* <u>Vestibular duct</u>

* Reissner membrane

* <u>Cochlear duct</u>

* Basilar membrane: thin at the basal end and wide at the apical end; supports <u>organ of Corti</u>

* <u>Tympanic duct</u>

* Bone

* Function: transformation of airborne vibrations into auditory neural signals

* Stria vascularis: produces <u>potassium</u>-rich endolymph for the <u>scala media</u>, which is essential for the endocochlear potential

* The <u>cochlear duct</u> (<u>scala media</u>) contains <u>hair</u> cells .

* These are specialized cells situated on a <u>basilar membrane</u>.

* They have apical modifications called <u>stereocilia</u>.

* Vibrations lead to stimulation of a specific location on the <u>basilar membrane</u>, depending on the <u>sound frequency</u> (tonotopy).

* High-frequency sounds stimulate <u>hair</u> cells at the base of the <u>cochlea</u>; the <u>basilar membrane</u> in this area is thin and rigid.

* Low-frequency sounds stimulate <u>hair</u> cells at the apex of the <u>cochlea</u> near an area called <u>helicotrema</u>; the <u>basilar membrane</u> in this area is wide and flexible.

* Auditory pathway :
1. * Auditory neural signals are detected by the <u>hair</u> cells of the organ of Corti, which are innervated by the bipolar <u>neurons</u> of the cochlear or spiral ganglion (first-order <u>neuron</u>).
2. * The signals are transmitted to the <u>ventral</u> and <u>dorsal</u> <u>cochlear nuclei</u> (second-order <u>neuron</u>) via the <u>axons</u> of the bipolar <u>neurons</u>, which constitute the cochlear part of the <u>vestibulocochlear nerve</u> (auditory nerve).
3. * The pathway diverges into the following parts:

* Direct pathway: <u>Axons</u> of the <u>dorsal</u> <u>cochlear nucleus</u> <u>neurons</u> join the <u>contralateral</u> <u>lateral lemniscus</u> and reach the <u>neurons</u> of the <u>inferior colliculus</u> (third-order <u>neurons</u>) on the other side.

* Indirect pathway:

* <u>Axons</u> of the <u>ventral</u> <u>cochlear nucleus</u> <u>neurons</u> reach the <u>superior olivary nucleus</u> (third-order <u>neuron</u>) on the <u>ipsilateral</u> and <u>contralateral</u> sides.

* <u>Axons</u> of the <u>neurons</u> of the <u>superior olivary nucleus</u> join the <u>lateral lemniscus</u> and <u>synapse</u> on the <u>neurons</u> of the <u>inferior colliculus</u> (fourth-order <u>neurons</u>).
4. * <u>Axons</u> of the <u>neurons</u> of the <u>inferior colliculus</u> <u>synapse</u> on the cells of the <u>medial geniculate body</u> (fourth-order or fifth-order <u>neuron</u>).
5. * <u>Axons</u> of the <u>neurons</u> of the <u>medial geniculate body</u> ascend the <u>posterior</u> limb of the <u>internal capsule</u>, where they form the auditory radiations, after which they reach <u>primary auditory cortex</u> (<u>superior temporal gyrus</u> in the <u>temporal lobe</u>) and <u>amygdala</u>.
6. * The <u>primary auditory cortex</u> connects to auditory association cortex.

> [!NOTE]
> <u>Loop diuretics</u> are <u>ototoxic</u> because they act on both the Na/K/2Cl carrier in the <u>ascending loop of Henle</u> of the <u>kidneys</u> and the same transporters in the <u>stria vascularis</u> of the <u>cochlea</u>. This effect can lead to <u>edema</u> of cochlear tissues, a decrease of the cochlear electrical potential, and temporary or permanent <u>sensorineural hearing loss</u>.




#### Vestibular system




* The system of balance and spatial orientation

* Consists of

* <u>Otolith organs</u>: fluid-filled pouches lined with sensory <u>epithelium</u> (maculae acusticae) 

* Utricle: senses motions in the <u>horizontal plane</u> (e.g., forward-backward, left-right movements)

* Saccule: senses motions in the <u>sagittal plane</u> (e.g., up-down movement)

* Three semicircular canals (horizontal, superior, and <u>posterior</u> <u>semicircular canals</u>): sense rotary movements (i.e., angular <u>accelerations</u>) at their dilated ends (i.e., crista ampullaris or <u>ampullary crest</u>)

* Specialized cells known as vestibular <u>hair</u> cells transduce minute displacements into neural signals that are then transmitted to the <u>brain stem</u> via the vestibular part of the <u>vestibulocochlear nerve</u> (see <u>vestibular pathway</u>).

## Embryology

* <u>Outer ear</u>

* <u>Auricle</u>: arises from the fusion of six auricular hillocks

* <u>External auditory meatus</u>: arises from <u>ectoderm</u> of 1st <u>pharyngeal cleft</u>

* <u>Middle ear</u>

* <u>Pharyngeal arch 1</u> (<u>mesoderm</u>): <u>incus</u>, <u>malleus</u>, <u>tensor tympani muscle</u>, <u>CN V</u>

* <u>Pharyngeal arch 2</u> (<u>mesoderm</u>): <u>stapes</u>, <u>stapedius muscle</u>, <u>CN VII</u>

* <u>Pharyngeal pouch</u> 1 (<u>endoderm</u>): <u>eustachian tube</u> and <u>middle ear</u> cavity

* <u>Tympanic membrane</u>: inner layer (<u>endoderm</u>), middle layer (<u>mesoderm</u>), outer layer (<u>ectoderm</u>)

* <u>Inner ear</u>: develops from the otic placode, a thickening of the <u>ectoderm</u>, which invaginates to form auditory <u>vesicles</u> or otocysts

* Otocysts form the <u>membranous labyrinth</u>:

* <u>Utricle</u> and <u>saccule</u> (contain sensory <u>hair</u> cells)

* <u>Cochlear duct</u> (contains <u>organ of Corti</u> and endolymph), endolymphatic duct (connects the <u>utricle</u> and <u>saccule</u> with the endolymphatic sac), and <u>semicircular canals</u>

* Vestibular and cochlear ganglions of <u>CN VIII</u>

* Otic capsule: A <u>mesenchymal</u> <u>cartilaginous</u> shell around the otic <u>vesicle</u> that develops into the <u>bony labyrinth</u>.

## Clinical significance

* <u>Retroauricular hematoma</u>

* <u>Otitis externa</u>

* <u>Acute otitis media</u>

* <u>Otosclerosis</u>

* <u>Chronic otitis media</u>

* <u>Cholesteatoma</u>

* <u>Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo</u>

* Ménière disease

* <u>Vestibular neuritis</u>

* <u>Hearing loss</u>

* <u>Ear barotrauma</u>

* <u>Tinnitus</u>

* Microtia

* A congenital deformity of the ear (i.e., the auricles) characterized by underdevelopment of the <u>pinna</u> and <u>hearing</u> impairment.

* <u>Microtia</u> varies in severity and can occur as an isolated <u>birth</u> defect or as part of a syndrome (e.g., <u>Treacher-Collins syndrome</u>).

* Anotia: a congenital ear deformity characterized by the complete absence of the <u>pinna</u> and <u>hearing</u> impairment
